chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: The septet at Manitou Beach, Goldkette and the Cottonpickers name (repeat)
summary: Jackson retells how Goldkette heard the seven-piece band at Clark's Lake, had Redman enlarge it, and gave it the Cotton Pickers name and Victor contract in 1927.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: What's the first name of the McKinney Cottonpickers?
Seven pieces, and they used to play up to Manitou Beach, Michigan, every summer. The guys would get out of school and they'd go up there and play.
What school were they getting out of?
Like Springfield. Some of the guys -- a couple of guys were still in high school, like Dave Wilburn, you know, and Claude was going to Wilberforce, you

know, and the guys used to play little gigs around there. So they got this job up in Manitou Beach, Michigan, to Clark's Lake. They used to go up there every summer. So Jean Goldkette heard this band, the seven pieces, and he liked what he heard. So at that time Don Redman was writing for Jean Goldkette. He was making arrangements for Jean Goldkette's orchestra, also writing for Whiteman. And I think I told this story before, I'm not sure, and he got Don to come out to Detroit and to take this band and enlarge on it to an 11 piece band, and he made it the house band in the Graystone.
And in those days, in order for -- you know, you're a black band, so they got to give you a name so that the people really know you're a black band.

And the band sounded so pretty on the radio and everything, you wouldn't recognize it as a black band, really, because they had so much finesse, so much quality. So they called it McKinney Cottonpickers, and the guys hadn't even been South. The band started in Detroit. And Jean Goldkette got them a contract with Victor Records. They named them the house band of the Graystone and they broadcast on WJR.
To me it turned out to be one of the greatest dance bands in the business. In fact, --
